extracted.intended_audience: legal academics, policymakers, patent practitioners, and biotech stakeholders
extracted.subtask_description: Analyze legal standards, empirical effects, and policy options for gene patent eligibility in U.S. law and propose a narrowly tailored legislative fix (patentability of mutant human gene variants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: To acquire a patent the invention must: fall within patent-eligible subject matter (§101), be useful (§101), novel (§102), nonobvious (§103), and adequately disclosed (§112).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note repeatedly cites these statutory requirements and explains that applicants must satisfy subject matter eligibility and the traditional utility/novelty/nonobviousness/enablement/written-description requirements; PTO rejections are appealable to PTAB and the Federal Circuit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject-matter exceptions: 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas'
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts exclude from patent eligibility 'laws of nature, natural phenomena, and abstract ideas'—these cannot be patented in the abstract.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although foundational principles are excluded, courts may find inventions patent-eligible if the claimed patent applies the basic scientific principle in some inventive way (see Mayo/Alice framework).

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (usefulness)
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention must serve some specific, presently known purpose (utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Brenner v. Manson: utility requires a specific, presently known use; applied here to require that claimed genetic inventions demonstrate practical utility (e.g., diagnostic relevance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The innovation must not have been previously discovered and disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory §102 standard; patent applicants must show the claimed subject matter is new relative to prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention must represent a significant advancement—not be obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory §103 standard (Graham v. John Deere); applied to assess whether genetic discoveries warrant patents beyond known research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure / written description and enablement (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicants must disclose the invention so others skilled in the art can replicate it and must precisely stake out what is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adequate disclosure is a statutory requirement and guards against overbroad claims that would stifle follow-on research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive application / 'inventive concept' (Mayo/Alice framework)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that touches a law of nature or abstract idea must include an 'inventive concept' in its application to be patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note cites Mayo and Alice: applying an abstract principle in a routine or conventional way is insufficient (Flook), while transformative/practical applications can be patentable (Diehr).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of man-made biological products (Chakrabarty 'made by man' test)
rubrics_metrics.description: Biological organisms or products that do not occur in nature because they are 'made by man' can fall outside the natural phenomenon exclusion and be patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diamond v. Chakrabarty supports broad construction—'anything under the sun that is made by man'—used to justify patenting genetically engineered organisms that do not occur naturally.

rubrics_metrics.name: European approach: DNA sequences patentable with industrial application (Directive 98/44/EC)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the EU, DNA sequences are inventions (not mere discoveries) so long as the claimed sequence has an industrial application such as use in diagnosis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note cites the EPO/EPC and Directive 98/44/EC as a narrowly tailored model allowing gene patents conditioned on industrial application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research-use exception (narrow judicial construction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Uses of patented inventions for some research purposes may be an exception, but U.S. courts have construed the research-use exception narrowly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: university research often held to further business objectives (Madey v. Duke); statutory exceptions like §271(e)(1) are limited; thus the Note treats the research-use exception as unreliable protection for follow-on research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent infringement defenses: invalidity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: An accused infringer can defend by arguing the patent is invalid for failure to meet patentability requirements (subject matter, novelty, nonobviousness, disclosure).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invalidity is a common defense; Myriad itself is an example where patents were invalidated under subject-matter grounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to exclude and patent term
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent grants the holder the right to exclude others from making, using, selling, or importing the patented invention for a limited period (currently twenty years).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents create exclusivity intended to incentivize investment, but the limited term is part of the statutory bargain (disclosure in exchange for time-limited monopoly).

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy balance: incentive vs. innovation
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent law must strike a balance between providing incentives (monopolies) to inventors and avoiding overbroad protection that stifles follow-on innovation and research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the central normative criterion the Note uses to evaluate gene patent regimes: too much protection can hinder science; too little can chill investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic stability / predictability as a criterion for reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Legislative or judicial changes should promote economic certainty to encourage investment in biotech; reforms that inject uncertainty deter investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note argues for incremental, narrow legislative fixes rather than sweeping overhauls or uncertain judicial reversals to restore investor confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Narrow legislative solution: allow patenting of mutant variants of human genes
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress should pass a narrow amendment to §101 explicitly recognizing mutant variants of human genes as patent-eligible subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposal: limit eligibility to specific disease-causing mutations (not whole genes), to promote investment while preserving research access and avoiding pandemic-related risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement that patented mutations be clinically relevant / tied to a disease (specific-mutation utility)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents on gene variants should be limited to specific mutations that the applicant has shown to be associated with a disease (demonstrable utility).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirrors pre-Myriad practice and prevents granting broad claims absent clinical relevance; does not impose extra burdens beyond pre-Myriad requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent overbroad claims: disallow claiming entire genes from single mutation discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims should not permit an inventor to claim an entire gene based on discovering a single mutation; claims must be mutation-specific.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limiting claims to specific mutations addresses concerns that a single discovery could foreclose further research on the overall gene.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclude nonhuman genes and pathogen genomes from eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy should exclude animal genes and pathogen genomes (e.g., viral genomes) from patent eligibility to protect basic research and pandemic response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By limiting patent eligibility to human gene mutations, basic animal-model research and pathogen-genome research remain free from patent monopolies that could impede urgent public-health responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade secrets are an inadequate alternative
rubrics_metrics.description: Relying on trade secret protection for genetic discoveries is a poor fit because trade secrets are unstable and discourage disclosure and dissemination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trade secret protection lasts only while secrecy is maintained and incentivizes withholding information—unlike patents that require disclosure and provide predictable protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risks of broad congressional overhauls or creating a new gene-specific patent regime
rubrics_metrics.description: Sweeping legislative overhauls (e.g., reversing Myriad wholesale) or creating an entirely new field of patent law for genetics would introduce significant uncertainty and prolonged litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note favors incremental, narrowly tailored amendments (EU-style carveouts) over broad statutory changes that could unsettle markets and reignite litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical impact of Myriad as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical studies about Myriad's aftermath—investment decline, abandoned diagnostics, and mixed effects on research—are used to evaluate the costs and benefits of current subject-matter rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note cites studies indicating reduced investor willingness and abandoned tests as justificatory evidence for policy change, while acknowledging some studies found limited research impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs and capital intensity of genetic research as justification for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: High fixed costs (sequencers, lab infrastructure) and capital needs for taking discoveries through to diagnostics and treatments justify some patent protection to attract investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note notes sequencing equipment costs and the long pipeline from discovery to market as reasons investors require predictable IP protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent prosecution and appeal pathway (USPTO, PTAB, Federal Circuit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applications proceed through the USPTO and rejected claims can be appealed to the PTAB and the Federal Circuit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The institutional review path affects predictability and enforcement; policy must account for how courts and agencies implement eligibility rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement concerns: aggressive enforcement can stymie research
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent holders who aggressively enforce gene patents can inhibit further research and diagnostics development, an enforcement risk to be considered when designing eligibility rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Note stresses that even with patents, scope and limits must be calibrated to prevent research chilling effects (supports narrow eligibility).
